en: (1a) 1 Oṃ, salutations to the venerable Guru!
[I bow to] that which is eternally attached within the lotus of the *brahmarandhra*, pure and marvelous.
I worship the lotus at the *dvādaśānta*, adorned by the stalks of the trembling *kuṇḍalinī*.

(1) Within the hollow of its sprouting interior, I worship the abode of the Goddess, which is marked by the corners and possesses the nature of a circle of ploughs indicated by the lines beginning with the letter 'a' joined together. (2)

Within the hollow of that [lotus], I meditate in my heart upon the body consisting of consciousness, which possesses the rosy luster of rubies bowing before a swarm of bees that are flashes of brilliant lightning; it is the mandala of the jewel-throne of *bindu* and *nāda*.
It is the abode of Brahman, encompassed by the play of the upward-pointing crest of the sacrificial fire.
I contemplate the primordial pair of swans (*haṃsa*) who have become the great remedy for the universal devouring of the Great Calamity (*mahotkata*).
Therein, within the lotus-feet of the Lord, which are overflowing with streams as red as saffron, (4) [1b]...

She remembers her mind, the abode of auspiciousness, which is cooled by the touch of moonbeams like a root-creeper, and which is the source of joy. She remembers her feet, upon which jeweled sandals are set, from which the clamor of sin is restrained,
which are as red as shimmering young shoots, and from whose nails radiates a brilliant luster.

I worship the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru situated upon my head, which shines like a blooming lotus arisen from the lake of supreme nectar. [6] This hymn of the Five Pādukās has emerged from the five faces.

It bestows the fruit of the glorious fivefold tradition (pañcāmnāya) and is exceedingly rare in this world. 8. Thus ends the instruction on the Glorious Guru in the fifth section of the Śrī Rudrayāmala.
1. Homage to the venerable Guru.
Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Asanā, Aghora, Gaurīśa, Trīśa, Mitrīśa, and thereafter Kapilānanda-guru.
Siddhiśāsana, Piṅga by name, and the man Puṣpadantaka;
then Śānti, known as Ugra, and the Guru named Pañcārtha;
Vidyācārya, Vratācārya, Dūrvāsas, and Kauśika are considered [the lineage].
Jaigīṣavya, Vratācārya, Kauṇḍinyācārya,
as well as those known as the eight Bhairavas, Aṅgāraka, Guru, Viśvanātha, Someśa, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvarūpaka.
Gaṅgādhara-guru and likewise Śrīśaṅkara-guru;
with the words "Nārāyaṇa-pada-anta," he is praised as the venerable embodiment of Vārādi, the preeminent teacher Śrī Vimalānanda-guru.
(2b) By the grace of their feet, Rāmānanda became renowned;
from him, who was devoted to the feet of his guru, came the one known as Bhairavānanda.
These indeed have been declared in their proper sequence as the lineage of the Pāśupata teachers.
Through the conjunction of their respective powers, Nāmāmbā and Padāntikā—
both granting boons and fearlessness— are the entirety of the lineage of the Śiva-teachers.

Whoever recites the lineage of the Gurus (gurukrama) with faith at the three junctions of the day shall obtain infinite fruit from [the performance of] ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, recitation (japa), and so forth. 8.
Thus ends the Śrīpāśupata Gurukrama.
1. Oṃ, salutations to Śiva.
Salutations to you, the stainless God; salutations to you whose form is knowledge;
salutations to you who are the embodiment of light and partless; let there be salutations to you. 1.
The light, pierced by the solar orb, abides in the foundation;
above the lunar wheel and further beyond that is the worship of Śiva. (2)
One should assume the unsurpassed lotus posture (padmāsana) as one's own seat;
there, having established the seat of mantra, one should perform the auspicious seat of the five spirits (pañcapretāsana).
I shall now describe breath control (prāṇāyāma); one should recite the mantra while focused upon one's own foundational center (svādhāra).

Brahmā is the inhalation (pūraka) of that [prāṇa], while Viṣṇu is the deity of the retention (kumbhaka). The exhalation (recaka) has the nature of fire, and one should draw it forth through the power of Śiva.
The western-facing liṅga is the sphere of Brahmā, which is the inhalation.
The most excellent practitioner should constantly practice the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
O Great Goddess, it removes sin—this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
Listen, O Goddess, to the great reality, as well as the other [topic], the vessel for the offering water (arghapātra).
O Goddess, the fire-wheel situated in the *mūlādhāra* is difficult to attain.
(7) [It is] the power (*śakti*) residing in the womb of fire, whose form consists of ten digits (*kalā*).
The giver of grace and fearlessness, whose form is fire and who is a great festival,
dwells eternally within the heart; O Great Goddess, he is the twelvefold, beautiful wheel of the sun, together with his most splendid Śakti.
O Great Goddess, she has two arms and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
thus, O Supreme Sovereign, she is Bālārka, possessing all these qualities.
O Goddess, she is established within the universe, the Supreme Mother whose form is nectar.
O Great Goddess of the Moon-wheel, [I bow to] the sixteen deities who are the Śaktis.
(11) To Amṛteśvarī Mahādevī, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is adorned with ornaments of pearls—homage be to you for the sake of nectar! (12)
Having struck the upper channel by contracting the lower channel,
and having taken hold of the middle channel, one should satisfy the supreme Khecarī. (4a) 13.
This has been told to you, O Goddess, which is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
Thus, the best of practitioners should worship this great reality (mahātattva).
The Goddess is mounted upon Prāṇa, and Mādana is joined with Śakra.
The neutral Śiva and Agni, adorned with the fourth vowel,
together with Ākāśa, the half-moon, and Nāda— this is the single light of the great festival.
Facing west, one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess who resides within it.
Resembling the deep red of the dawn, possessing a noose, a goad, and three eyes,
and bearing a skull-cup, a thunderbolt, and the beautiful fire-wheel— this goddess,
whose form brings delight through desire, stands outside the corners.
Salutations to you, Kāmeśvarī, the great goddess who is the power of Rudra.
(18) [I bow to] Prāṇa, seated upon the throne of the Goddess and united with Kandarpa-Śiva.
O Great Goddess, the Thousand-eyed One, [the syllable] *prāṇa* and likewise *agni*,
joined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the bindu and the crescent moon—
this is the Kāmarāja, O Great Goddess, which brings about the agitation of the world. (19–20)
The Goddess, resembling a ripe bimba fruit, holding a bow, arrows, and other weapons, bearing a noose and a goad, and likewise holding a mātuluṅga fruit;
the Goddess seated upon the solar disc, and likewise the Jālandhara-pīṭha.
O Vajreśvarī, obeisance to you, the great goddess who is the power of Viṣṇu.
(22) O Goddess, one should join the seed-syllable of Indra mounted upon Madana;
below that, Śambhu and Agni, adorned with the Bindu, Khaṇḍendu, and Ardhendu. (23)
The Great Goddess Śaktibīja is adorned with the fourth vowel;
the Great Goddess Trikūṭa is Mahātripurasundarī. (24)
The Great Goddess has four arms and three eyes, resembling ten million moons; she holds a book and a rosary, with her hands raised holding a noose and a goad.
The Great Goddess [also holds] the lunar disc, which is as enchanting as the Pūrṇa-pīṭha.
O Great Goddess, the Power of Brahman, O Mistress of the Yoni, salutations be unto you!
(26) Having extracted the three peaks, one should draw forth the three-deity syllable;
it is the Great Goddess of the fourth seed-syllable, adorned by the lunar orb of the Brahma-fragment. (27)
This great mantra-vidyā is the Supreme Mother (Parāmbā) in the form of Śakti;
she is the Goddess established as a single peak-syllable (kūṭa), bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
She is the seat of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree.
(5b) She holds a noose, a goad, and a third eye, and wields five arrows and a bow;
she eternally resides within the Brahma-wheel and has the nature of the power of gnosis (jñānaśakti).
Oḍiyāna Mahādevī, salutations to you for the sake of good fortune.
(30) Having performed mental recitation, the fruit of ten million recitations is obtained.
The Liṅga facing west bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (31)
You are the Mother of the three worlds; you alone are the all-pervading one. You alone are the principle of Śiva, and you alone are the essence of all vows.
You alone are all sacred fords, and you alone are the essence of all mantras. (32)
You alone are all the gods; you alone are the embodiment of power.
O Goddess, you are the remover of disease and sorrow, and the warder-off of obstacles.
Ignorance attains knowledge, which destroys suffering and poverty.
(34) One should offer bali to the five elements, and likewise perform self-worship;
having meditated upon the five pretas, one should offer food to the consumer of oblations (the fire). (35)
Listen, O Goddess, to this great knowledge, the consciousness that is eternal in all things;
for him in whose heart it arises, knowledge becomes certain.
Even now, O Goddess, you alone are my refuge; you alone are my shelter.
O Maheśvarī, grant, grant whatever desire one constantly prays for! 37.
Thus ends the *Jyotisānanda-stava*.
Victory to the form of the Śrī-guru!
The venerable Lord said: Having recited the *kullukā* mantra over the head, one should project the *setu* into the heart;
for the purification of the great *setu*, however, one should withdraw it into the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
(6b) In Maṇipūra, however, is Nirvāṇa; below is Mahākuṇḍalinī.
Svādhiṣṭhāna is Kāmarāja, and Rākinī is situated at the crown of the head. 2.

Having contemplated [the path] according to the rule, O Goddess, situated near the *mūlādhāra*, one should repeatedly remember it, O Goddess, as being thinner than a fiber of lotus-stalk, extending up to the end of the *viśuddha* [cakra], reaching the abode of the Goddess,
and encircled by the root mantra, like a double-tongued serpent.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, what is the Kullakā like? O God, what is the Setu like?
What is the Mahāsetu like, and what is Nirvāṇa like?
"O Lord, tell me what kind of birth was described by Anyārva.
Śrī Īśvara said:
"O Goddess, this which is more secret than the secret is told out of affection for you."
O Maheśānī, without which recitation and other practices are indeed fruitless;
O Goddess, Mahānīlasarasvatī is the *kullukā* of Tārā.

The five-syllabled *kullukā* of Kālikā is thus described. O Parameśvarī, [the syllables] Kālī, Kurccavadhū, Māyā, and the word ending in *pha* constitute the eight-syllabled *kullukā* of Chinnamastā, O Maheśānī. (7–8)
And for Vajravairocanī, one should proclaim the *anta* and *verma*.
For Bhairavī, who bestows the state of prosperity (*saṃpatpada*), the *kullukā* is considered to be the first [syllable].
The *kullukā* of Śrī Tripurasundarī consists of twelve syllables.
The first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, followed immediately by Kāmarāja;
then after that is Lajjābīja, and Tripurā follows next. Afterward, one should extract the word "Bhagavatī," and then the pair of "Dante. (10–11)
"O Goddess, this Saṃjapā Kullukā has been declared to you by me.
Now, therefore, I shall explain it further; listen to that, O Priyaṃvadā. (12)
Without knowledge of which, recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites become fruitless;
for Brahmins, the Praṇava is the bridge, and likewise for Kṣatriyas;
for Vaiśyas it is the *phaṭ* syllable, while for Śūdras it is said to be *Māyā*.

And the Great Bridge (mahāsetu), O Queen of Gods, belongs to Sundarī Bhuvaneśvarī. The seed-syllable of Kālikā is that of Tārā, while the seed-syllable of Kūrcaka is the seed-syllable of Vadhū at the end, O lady of beautiful countenance, [which constitutes] the Great Bridge.
Having first recited the Mahāsetu, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
Blessed, blessed is he who is equal to Śukra in speech and like the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) himself;
in battle he is like Kṛtānta (Yama), and among women he is like Madana (Kāma).
(8a) At the time of recitation, he shall [attain] it at all times; of this there is no doubt.
Now I shall speak of Nirvāṇa; listen attentively, O sinless one!
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then recite the *mātṛkā*. Then, O Maheśānī, one should utter the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and then the *vāgbhava* [bīja].
One should then recite the entire *mātṛkā* once more and utter the *praṇava*.
Thus, O Īśānī, one should recite the mantra with the root syllable uttered in this manner during the inhalation;
for he who does not know this Nirvāṇa, O Goddess,
will find no success even in a hundred crores of years.

Therefore, with every effort, one should recite that unsurpassed mantra as prescribed by the Great Goddess and according to the rules of the teacher; within six months one attains perfection— of this there is no doubt.
He alone is the manifest sovereign of the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
He is the refuge, he is the knower of wisdom, and he is the knower of the truth of the mantra.
Let him alone wander upon the earth like one who remains at home in his own house.
By the mere sight of him, enemies are utterly destroyed.
Having thus donned the armor, whoever recites this king of mantras attains nirvāṇa; having likewise recited the *kullukā*, he overcomes worldly existence.
For them, that [state] is the very essence of existence; success and the goddesses are in their hands, affection is the end of their hearts, and their speech is like the lotus within a lotus.
25. Thus ends the Kullukā in the Rudrayāmala.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady!
If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is able to exercise his power.
Indeed, even a god cannot stir even a virtuous impulse toward a deity;
therefore, how can one who has not performed meritorious deeds be capable of bowing to, saluting, or praising you, who are worshipped even by Hari, Hara, Viriñci, and the rest? (1)
Viriñci, fashioning the worlds from the very subtle limb— the lotus born from your feet— creates the worlds without deficiency;
yet Śauri somehow bears it upon his thousand heads.
Having agitated this [world], Hara resorts to the practice of smearing himself with ashes.
She is the city on the island of the sun for the inner darkness of ignorance,
and the channel for the nectar of the blossoms of consciousness for those who are dull-witted.
(9a) For the poor, you are a wish-fulfilling gem; for those submerged in the ocean of birth, you are the tusk of the Boar, the supreme enemy of Mura. 3.

Other than you, the host of deities grants the boons of fearlessness with their two hands; you alone manifest the gestures of both the boon and fearlessness. You exist to protect from fear and to bestow even the most desired fruit.
Indeed, for you who are the refuge of the worlds, your two feet alone are skillful.
In ancient times, having worshipped you— the mother of good fortune for those who bow before her— the goddess Hari became a woman and brought even the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) to agitation.
Even Smara, having bowed to you, possesses a form that is to be licked by the eyes of Rati;
for he is indeed capable of inciting delusion even within the hearts of sages and throughout the worlds.
His bow is made of flowers, his string consists of bees, and he has five arrows.
(9b) While the neighboring king Vasanta and Dhanaratha, accompanied by the Malaya breeze, were present,
nevertheless, O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, you alone bestowed some indescribable compassion upon everyone.

From the corner of her eye, he obtained this world; thus the bodiless god of love triumphs. (6) She has a tinkling girdle-string, breasts like the frontal globes of a young elephant, a slender waist, and a face like the full autumn moon.
May the consort of the Destroyer of Cities (Puramathituh)—who holds a bow, arrows, a noose, and even a goad in her palms—stand before us; for she is indeed the city of the cuckoo (Ahoh Puruhpikā).
[May she stand] in the midst of the Ocean of Nectar, surrounded by a grove of celestial trees.
In the garden of the Nipa trees on Maṇidvīpa, within a house of wish-fulfilling gems,
upon a couch in the form of Śiva, she dwells reclining on the lap of Paramaśiva.
How many fortunate ones indeed worship you, O Hari, who are the bliss of consciousness! Though you are one,
you reside as the Earth in the *mūlādhāra*, as Fire in the *maṇipūra*, as Air in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and as Space in the heart above.
The mind also, having pierced the entire path of the *kula* right between the eyebrows,
dwells in secret with its Lord in the thousand-petaled lotus.
With showers of streams of nectar trickling from within Your lotus feet—
Again, sprinkling the manifold world of conceptual proliferation with the splendor of the tradition of aesthetic essence,
you reach your own ground— a hollowed-out family-pit shaped like a serpent with exceedingly hot coils— and having made yourself your own self, you sleep there. 10.
With four Śrīkaṇṭhas and five Śiva-yuvatis below—
thus with nine, who are the primordial natures (mūlaprakṛtis)— they have taken refuge in Śambhu.

O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, the corners of your abode have been transformed into the three concentric circles of the forty-three-petaled lotus, together with the three lines. Your beauty, however, is beyond description.
Even the lords of poets, such as Brahmā and others, can somehow manage [to describe it],
when the celestial nymphs, out of longing for the world, go in their minds toward the state of union with Śiva— a goal difficult to attain even through austerities. (12)
Hundreds of women— letting down their braided hair and casting off the garments from their jar-like breasts— run after Nārada, the son of Narma, as he falls within the range of your sidelong glance;
he who is the very essence of the rainy season and whose beauty is a delight to the eyes.
The young women, their girdles forcibly slipping and their fine silken garments falling away,
[fell] fifty-six upon the earth and fifty-two more in the water. (13) (11a) Fifty-six on the ground and fifty-two in the water.
Sixty-two rays in the sacrificial fire, fifty-four in the wind,
thirty-six in the heavens, and sixty-four in the mind—
above even those rays stands the pair of your lotus feet. (14)
Having bowed but once to you— who are as radiant as the autumnal moonlight, who wear a crown of matted locks joined with the moon,
and who hold in your hands a water-lily, a protective amulet of crystal, and a book—
the presence of the virtuous can never be attained by any other means.
The words of the lords of poets are like grapes sweetened with honey;
only a few virtuous ones resort to you, who possess the ruddy luster of the morning sun upon the forest of the hearts of those great poets.
(11b) These [sages], whose speech is as captivating as the youthful amorous play of the beloved of Viriñci, delight the assembly with their profound words. || 16 ||
O Sahajāmbā, he who meditates upon you together with Vaśinī and the other [Śaktis], whose splendor resembles the shards of moonstone and who are the progenitors of speech—
becomes a composer of great poems, rendered beautiful by their varied stylistic turns.
With words as sweet as nectar, the Goddess of Speech delights in her lotus-like mouth.
He who, by the radiance of his body— the very path to Fortune— remembers the entire sky and the earth as if submerged in rubies, like the newly risen sun.
How many celestial courtesans, together with Urvaśī, have not become submissive to him— their eyes possessing the modest charm of startled forest deer? (18) (12a)

Having formed the face as a *bindu* and the pair of breasts beneath it, one should meditate below that upon the half of the letter *ha*, O Consort of Hara—the digit of Love. This very quickly brings about the immediate agitation of a woman; thus it is exceedingly swift.

He who holds you in his heart like a statue carved from moonstone— she who, with the sun and moon as her pair of breasts, swiftly causes even the three worlds to whirl about, and who scatters from her limbs a mass of rays that are the essence of nectar.
It quells the pride of those afflicted by serpents, like the king of birds;
seeing one scorched by fever, it brings comfort with a shower of nectar-drops.
It is slender as a streak of lightning, yet composed of the sun, the moon, and fire.
Great souls, beholding with minds that have crushed the impurities of illusion your digit seated above six lotuses within the expanse of the Great Lotus,
experience a wave of supreme bliss. (21)
"O Bhavānī, you who are my slave, bestow upon me a compassionate glance"— thus,
how could there be any desire to praise her as "Bhavānī, you"? [For she is already mine.]
At that very moment, you bestow upon him the state of union with yourself,
whose feet are clearly honored by the crowns of Mukunda, Brahmā, and Indra;
for you have taken away his body while your own mind remained unsatisfied.
I suspect that even the other half of Śambhu’s body has been taken away;
for indeed, your entire form is reddish-hued, possesses three eyes, is bent by your breasts, and bears a crown with a curved crescent moon. (23)
The Creator (Brahmā) procreates the world, Hari protects it, and Rudra destroys it;
yet the Lord (Īśa), casting that [triple form] aside, even conceals his own body.
Thus, while the former [three] are always [active], Śiva alone bestows grace upon all this.

O Śivā, although you are composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), you are the source of the three gods; for they rely solely upon your command, as expressed by your creeper-like eyebrows which quiver in an instant. (24)
Let that which is fashioned as worship at your two feet be true worship;
for indeed, standing ever near the jeweled pedestal that supports your feet, these [gods] have their crowns and ear-ornaments perpetually bowed in salutation. (25)
Brahmā goes to his fivefold end; Hari attains cessation;
the Destroyer meets his destruction; and Kubera goes to his demise.
Even the vast expanse of the eyes of Indra’s consort, free from sleep, closes its lids.
While this great dissolution prevails, your husband remains here;
his every repetition of mantras, his speech, his crafts, and even the formation of all ritual gestures—
May whatever movement I have, my circumambulation, the ritual of offering oblations to the fire,
my prostration, my reclining, and all my happiness— may all this, in the state of self-surrender, become a synonym for worship unto You. (27)
While you, like Lord Īśāna, incessantly bestow prosperity upon the destitute,
your foot— so beautiful as a cluster of mandāra blossoms— scatters the nectar of its bouquet of loveliness; yet, [even] upon this foot of yours...

Plunging into it with their very lives through the six modes of conduct, they attain the state of the six classes of beings. Yet, even the gods beginning with Brahmā and Indra, though they consume the nectar that wards off fear, old age, and death, all perish when their allotted time is exhausted.
O Mother, the power of your earrings is such that even for Śambhu—who has devoured the formidable field [of the universe]—there is no end to his hunger; yet for you, it is the root of satisfaction.
Setting aside the crown of Brahmā before him, [the earrings surpass] the slayer of Kaiṭabha.
Victorious is the remark made by your attendants when Hara rises to greet you as you forcefully advance toward their abode, where the heavy crown has slipped from his firm, high tiara. (29)
(14a) Having encompassed the entire world through sixty-four tantras,
Paśupati then became dependent upon the expansion of various specific attainments (*siddhi*).
Furthermore, due to your persistent request, this independent *tantra*— which accomplishes all human goals (*puruṣārtha*)—
was brought down to the surface of the earth by you.
Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Earth, then the Sun, and the Moon.
O Mother, these letters— *smara*, *haṃsa*, *śakra*, and thereafter *parā*, *māra*, and *hari*—
joined at their endings with the three *hṛllekhās*,
attain the status of being parts of Your name. (31)
Some, who delight in the flavor of eternal and boundless great enjoyment, having placed this triad— Smara, Yoni, and Lakṣmī— at the forefront of their minds,
chant your names with rosaries strung with wish-fulfilling gems.
(14b) Offering oblations of hundreds of streams of fragrant clarified butter into the auspicious fire,
you are the body of Śambhu, whose pair of breasts are the moon and the sun.
O Blessed One, I bow to you, whose self is the ninefold self (navātman) and who is free from all taint.

Therefore, this relationship between you two— between the dependent (śeṣa) and the support (śeṣin)— subsists by virtue of being common to both of you, who are intent upon the supreme bliss of the state of equal flavor (samarasa).
You are the mind, you are space, you are the wind, and you are the charioteer of the wind;
you are water and you are earth—for when you have undergone transformation, there is indeed nothing else.
It is you alone who, through your universal form, transform yourself.
I have taken refuge in the form of consciousness and bliss through my union with the youthful Śivā.
I bow to Your supreme weapon, which resides in the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*), possesses the luster of ten million suns and moons,
and is embraced on its sides by the Supreme Consciousness.
(15a) By propitiating him with all one's power— even though he is beyond the range of the sun, the moon, and needles—
mankind indeed dwells in a world of light within a realm that was once without light. || 35 ||
In the state of purity, I worship Śiva— the progenitor of the sky— who is as clear as pure crystal,
and also the Goddess, whose afflictions are equal to his,
and by whose departing luster the path to the likeness of moonbeams is traversed.

The world shines like a female cakora bird whose inner darkness has been shaken off. I worship that indescribable pair of swans belonging to the great ones, who dwell in Lake Mānasa and are singularly devoted to the nectar of the blossoming lotus of consciousness.
When the eighteenfold sciences reach their culmination through conversation with you, they yield every fault as a virtue, just as water yields milk from the ocean.
[This occurs] when you, remaining intent, preside over the fire within your own seat (the *svādhiṣṭhāna*).
I praise that Saṃvartā and that great Samayā, the Mother,
when the world is consumed by fire in the great conflagration of wrath.
Your glance, which bestows a cooling remedy,
[is like a cloud] possessing lightning through its flashing that opposes the darkness,
and bearing a rainbow formed by shimmering ornaments of various gems. (38)
I serve your dark cloud-like form, the sole refuge of Maṇipūra,
raining down upon the three worlds scorched by the sun that is Śiva.
At the root, which is your support, [I serve her] who is intent on the dance through the thousand-fold time.
I bow to the Ninefold Self, the dancer in the great cosmic theater of the nine aesthetic sentiments.
Through both of these [parents], who were graced by compassion for the sake of the dual ritual procedure, the entire world was brought forth in the sacrifice as the father and mother. 41.
(16a) Thus ends the Ānandalaharī Stotra.
[The sky] is densely constructed with the jewels of the firmament that have attained the state of rubies.
O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, who could possibly describe your golden crown, which, when close at hand, causes the mind to wonder:
"Is this a crescent moon variegated by its shimmering reflection, or is it the bow of Indra? (1)

O Śivā, may your mass of hair— dense, glossy, and smooth, its arrangement like a cluster of blossoming blue lotuses— dispel our darkness. It is for the sake of perceiving its innate fragrance that the flowers [of the gods] approach it.
I consider this to be a grove of trees belonging to the Destroyer of Bala;
for it bears vermilion, as if it were the fresh rays of the sun captured by the masses of light emanating from the darkness of her thick, braided hair.
May the wave of beauty of your face spread security for us, like the path of the parting line of hair, which is a channel for the overflow of its stream. (3)
Your face, surrounded by curling locks that naturally resemble young bees, puts to shame the splendor of the lotus; for when it smiles,
it is made beautiful by the filaments of the luster of its teeth.
The honey-bees of the eyes of the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) are intoxicated by its fragrance.
And this forehead of yours shines with a purity of loveliness and splendor;
I believe it to be a second fragment of the crescent moon upon his crown.
Through the relinquishing of error, having joined both together, they meet;
the full moon, a patchwork of nectar-plaster, transforms [into that very state].
O Mistress of the World, when your eyebrows are slightly arched in their addiction to shattering the fears of the universe,
I believe that the Lord of Rati holds a bow— strung with the virtue of your two bee-hued eyes—
and grasps it in his left hand.
O Umā, you conceal the space between them by covering [your eyes] with your forearm and fist.
Your left eye, being of the nature of the sun, produces the day;
at its end, it creates the mother of the three watches (the night) by becoming the lord of the night (the moon).
Your third glance, possessing the luster of a golden lotus scorched by fire,
assumes the character of twilight moving between the mass of day and night;
it is expansive, auspicious, clearly radiant, and worthy of the blue water-lily.
Your glance, an ocean of compassion, is somehow sweetly intoxicating; it is like a creeping vine of enjoyment, and like the city of Avantī, it triumphs over the vast expanse of many cities.
That name, certainly worthy of common usage, reigns supreme.
Her pair of ears, which delight solely in the nectar of the clusters of compositions of poets,
possess two earrings in the form of side-glances that are like restless bees.
Seeing that [face] of yours, which is agitated by the savoring of the nine rasas,
your forehead-eye, slightly reddened from contact with the fire of Vasu’s envy,
became intent on censuring Śiva when his face was moist with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra). || 9 ||

O Mother, your glance toward me is full of compassion; it is wrathful toward Gaṅgā, filled with wonder at the face of Giriśa, fearful of Hara’s serpents, and the producer of beauty for the lotus. It is well-beaming, O Friend, yet directed toward me. 10.
Having reached the shore of the ocean like Garuḍa spreading his wings, these two eyes—
possessing the power to shatter the cities [of the demons] and bearing the fruit of melting away the essence of tranquility from the mind of the Destroyer of Cities—
are like two lotus buds belonging to the lineage of the Lord of Mountains.
(18a) As he perceives [the moon] possessing the grace of Cupid’s arrow drawn back to the ear,
its three-fold coloration is distinguished by its blending with the quality of dark collyrium.
O beloved of Īśāna, this triad shines within your eyes:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who have ceased from their task of creating the gods once more; it is as if they were the three qualities—rajas, sattva, and tamas—bearing those very attributes. 12.
O Paśupati, whose heart is dependent on others, purify us with your compassionate eyes that possess the luster of red, white, and dark blue.
Surely this river is the Śoṇa, the Gaṅgā, and the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā).
O sinless one, you bring about the confluence of the three sacred streams.
O Aparṇā, in your ear, the fish— frightened by the whispering of the eyes of those chanting prayers—
surely hide within the water, their scales shimmering like jewels.
And this blue water-lily, its petals folded together like a door-panel,
opens at dawn and closes at night by means of its inherent power. (14)
O Daughter of the King of Mountains, those who revile you, saying that the world undergoes dissolution and emergence through your closing and opening of the eyes—
[they do not realize] that this entire world is born from your opening of the eyes and [returns] to dissolution [when they close them].
I suspect that your eyes have abandoned all hesitation in order to protect me.
O Śivā, with your long glance, which possesses the luster of a blue lotus crushed by a forest fire,
bathe even me, who am wretched and dwelling in a cave, with your compassion.
By this I am blessed, and there is no certainty of loss for you;
whether in the forest or in a palace, the moon sheds its rays with equal impartiality.
O daughter of the King of Serpents, your pair of hands is curved.
(19a) For whom does it not inspire the curiosity of the flower-arrowed god’s bow,
where it shines, having crossed the path of the ear and slanting across?
The side-glances of your eyes, intent upon the aim of an arrow, direct the mind toward the drawing of the shaft.
I consider this face of yours, with its four wheels— the pair of earrings reflected in the expanse of your quivering cheeks— to be the very essence of the sentiment of love.
Mounting his chariot made of wood— the earth— whose wheels are the sun and the moon,
the great hero Māra rushed toward the first husband who had already conquered [him].
This is a wave of nectar, a wave of excellence, consisting of the eloquent verses of Sarasvatī.
As you drink in all [these words] incessantly with the ladles of your ears,
the multitude of your earrings, their heads shaken by the wonder and praise,
seem to proclaim every composition with their loud jingling sounds. 19.
May this bridge of your nose, like a banner-cloth upon the lineage of the Snowy Mountains,
yield for us the fruit that is our due and is now near at hand.
Bearing within them pearls known by their exceedingly cool breaths,
and externally possessing pearl-like fruits through the abundance of their blossoms;
O fair-toothed one, [the trees] possess the luster of your lips, which are naturally red.
The coral creeper produces a fruit that creates an appearance of similarity [to your lip];
yet the Bimba fruit, reddened by the reflection of your own image, would somehow feel ashamed even to mount the scale to compete with it. (21)
As the cakora birds drank the mass of moonlight from your moon-like face,
their beaks became numbed by its excessive sweetness;
therefore, they possess the dull luster of waves of nectar from the cool-rayed moon.

Night after night, they drink [the moon] at will, mistaking it for sour gruel; they are rendered dull by the incessant repetition of their husband’s manifold virtues. (22) (20a) [She who is] numbed by the unremitting recital of her husband’s multitude of qualities.
O Mother, may your tongue, possessing the luster of the Java flower, be victorious!
For when you are seated upon it, the form of Sarasvatī—which is composed of crystal and silver—transforms into the body of ruby. 23.
Having conquered the Daityas in battle with hands that had seized the Śiva-missiles,
and having turned back those who were averse to the discarded floral offerings (nirmālya) of Caṇḍāṅga, Tripura-hara, and Nirmālya-vimukha—
[the city] was rendered white as the moon, cool camphor, and the gods Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra.
O Mother, fragments of betel from your mouth are being smeared [upon me].
While you were singing various pure praises of Paśupati, you began with words of approval as your head moved and your eyes flickered.
Your speech, having eclipsed the soft warbling of the female cuckoo with its own sweetness, mutes the newly strung lute of the Cōḷa king.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the face of Śambhu, which serves as a mirror, is held by his hand;
it was touched by the Snowy Mountain in the capacity of a year,
and raised up by the Lord of Mountains with composure while being held by the bearer of the mirror.
How can we describe your chin as being without comparison? Your neck, O subduer of cities, constantly embraced by his arms, bears the beauty of a lotus stalk for your lotus-like face. (26)
For she constantly wears a white necklace that, though soiled by the dust from the hooves of many horses, possesses the beauty of a lotus stalk;
and on her neck, O you who are uniquely skilled in the melodies and modulations of song, there are three lines. (27)
They shine forth as guarantors for the enumeration of the straight and excellent qualities acquired through marriage,
being mines of various kinds of sweet melodies.
As if they were the boundary lines demarcating the stability of three villages,
the four lotus-faces of the Lotus-Born praise the beauty of your four creeper-like arms, which are as soft as lotus stalks.
Trembling before the nails of the enemy of Andhaka, who had crushed Mada,
he offered his four heads with the intent of placing them as a hand of refuge;
[the heads] which, with the luster of their claws, seemed to mock the color of fresh lotuses.
Regarding the beauty of your hands, how can we possibly describe it?
Perhaps the lotus-hand might occasionally attain a semblance of equality with them, if its petals were reddened by the lac-dye from the soles of the feet of the Goddess of Fortune as she plays. (30)
O Goddess, may this pair of breasts of yours— equal [in size], drunk upon by the faces of the two moving elephants, and with their nipples ever protruding—
constantly remove your inner distress.
Upon seeing them, Heramba, his heart agitated by apprehension yet causing laughter,
suddenly and repeatedly touches those two breasts with his hand—
those breasts which are like jeweled jars filled with the essence of nectar. (31)
Those two sons of Manu, who have not yet experienced the tremor of doubt nor the banner of the Lord of Mountains,
are even now drinking [the nectar of existence], having never known the taste of union with a wife—
those two youths who are the subduers of the elephant-faced god and the demon Krauñca.
The expanse of her breasts bears a long necklace composed of pearls and gems, fashioned from the very forms of the frontal globes of the elephants of the quarters;
it is variegated within by the luster of the Vidyādharas.

O Daughter of the Mountain, I believe that your milk flows from your heart like the fame of a city-conqueror, mingled with his majesty. (33) (22a) I consider your breast-milk, O Daughter of the Earth-supporter, to be [such].
The milk flows like the Sarasvatī from its source to its mouth;
having tasted that which was given by you to the compassionate one, the young Dravidian became a charming composer of poetry for mature poets. (34)
O Daughter of the Mountain, the God of Love was swallowed by the deep channel of your navel with a body licked by the rows of flames from Śiva’s wrath;
from that [nave], a streak of smoke arose.
O Mother, people know that [line] as your line of body hair (romāvali).
O Śivā, O Mother, that which has the form of a wave upon the body of the Yamunā appears to the wise as something slender in your waist. 35–36.
From the mutual friction of their jar-like breasts, [the fragrance] arose within the space between them;
emerging from her body, it seemed as if it were entering the doe of her navel-cave.

O Girijā, your navel is something indescribable: it is a steady whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, a creeper of the line of hair upon the bud-like breasts, a basin for its own reservoir, and the sacrificial fire for the splendor of the flower-arrowed god of love; it is the pleasure-chamber of Rati.
Victorious is the flame of the fire of the eye of Giriśa, which brings about the cessation of worldly existence.
As her form gradually bends, the waist of her naturally slender body— situated between the slopes of her breasts— seems to break slowly upon the folds of her belly.

May there be well-being for you, O Daughter of the Mountain, whose middle has long since become like a river with its banks crumbling away, yet who remains in a state of equilibrium through the stability of your form.
May there be well-being for your breasts, which are now as fragile as cotton that is being squeezed and crushed until it perspires.
Drawing back at the base of his arms— which resemble golden jars—
the slender-bodied one clung to your belly to protect it from being broken.
O Goddess Parvati, as if with three folds like creeping vines, you are bound in three ways;
having severed from his own hips both weight and breadth, the Lord of Mountains placed them upon you in the form of an adornment.
Therefore, this vast and heavy mass of slopes covers the entire earth and yet brings it to lightness.
And for the lords of poets, the thick groves of golden plantain stalks are fierce.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having surpassed both [the gods and the poets] with your two beautiful thighs,
you have also conquered the pair of frontal globes of the elephant-like celestial poets with your two well-rounded knees, which are hardened by your husband’s prostrations.
Long ago, O Daughter of the Mountain, the flower-arrowed god repeatedly and most certainly attempted to conquer Rudra by placing two quivers filled with double the number of arrows within his shanks.
Those two feet of yours, upon which ten arrows appear at their tips—
disguised as the points of your toenails and uniquely sharpened by the crowns of the gods—
are worn by the crests of the Vedas as their final resting place.
O Mother, place these two feet of yours upon my head out of compassion—
those feet for which the water used for washing is the river flowing from the matted locks of Paśupati,
and for which the splendor of red lac is the luster of the crest-jewel of the youthful sun. 43.
The two [feet] of Himānī (the Snow-Goddess) are beautiful as they tread upon the slopes of the Himalayas;
they are lovely at night while she sleeps, and bright during the day;
they are the supreme vessel of fortune, creating prosperity for those who observe the sacred times.
O Mother, it is a wonder that your two lotus-feet should surpass [ordinary] lotuses here; what is more marvelous than this? We offer salutations to these feet, which delight the eyes;
we praise this pair, whose hands [of rays] are clearly radiant with the glow of red lac.
(24a) He who is the lord of beasts, who is extremely envious and longs to strike [them], [is found] in the pleasure-grove, the best place for sport. 45.
Having feigned a slip of the tongue regarding her lineage, she then, overcome with embarrassment,
strikes her husband on the forehead with her lotus-like feet—
thereby uprooting, after a long time, the internal thorn caused by burning grief.
With the tinkling of the tips of her scales, the enemy of Śiva (Viṣṇu) let out a triumphant roar.
O Goddess, how have the virtuous brought your feet— the abode of beauty and the non-abode of calamities— to a state comparable to the hard shell of a tortoise?
Or how was it that at the time of the wedding,
the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), with a compassionate mind, took [the mountain] and placed it upon the sacrificial stone?
With his nails, which were like moons causing the lotus-hands of the celestial women to close, he marked it.
Those divine trees seem to bear his feet with their own hands,
as they offer him fruits from the tips of their sprout-like fingers.

O Mother, tell me at what time may I, a seeker of knowledge, drink the water used for washing your feet— which has taken on the hue of red lac— and which bestows auspicious prosperity upon the poor without delay? 48.

When she bestows speech— which, by its very nature, is the cause of poetry even for the mute— upon the lotus-like faces of those who desire to attain the playful grace of poetic composition, it is as if she places betel-leaf within their mouths. (49)
Moving and sporting about, the palace-swan-like women do not leave her;
they teach her graceful gait through the pretext of the tinkling of their auspicious jeweled anklets, as she moves with beautiful conduct. || 50 ||
Curved in her hair, naturally slender at her waist, and possessing a gentle smile; having the hue of a *śirīṣa* flower in her heart, yet as hard as stone upon the slope of her breasts.
Extremely slender at the waist yet broad in the region of her noble hips,
a certain reddish compassion of Śambhu triumphs in order to protect the world. It is the inner sanctum of the Enemy of Tripura, with its dark-blue sky-like feet.
The disciplined observance of ritual service is difficult for those with restless senses to attain;
nevertheless, these immortals, headed by Indra, have achieved incomparable perfection by merely standing at the threshold of your doorway through the powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
O Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, and Īśvara, you have lost your status as couches;
Śiva is merely a deceptive coverlet fashioned from your own pure radiance,
which has turned reddish by receiving the reflection of your splendors.
(26a) Embodied as the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), he evokes curiosity in the eyes;
the spot [on the moon] is musk, and the lunar orb is composed of water. 53.
This emerald casket has been filled with precious gems and camphor;
therefore, by means of your enjoyment, its hollow interior becomes empty day after day, yet Brahmā surely fills it again and again for your sake. (54)

For one who always contemplates you, O Eternal One, as being served on all sides by the compassionate powers beginning with *aṇimā*, which have arisen from his own body— what wonder is there for him as he bears the abundant wealth of the Three-eyed Lord?
The great fire of universal destruction performs the rite of lustration for her;
and Kāmadeva, whose body possesses the splendor of a blossoming kadamba tree, laughs at the city of the breasts of the Great One as they emerge from her side-glances.
Madana produced a delusion in the mind of Hara;
O Umā, this is the ultimate result for those who are devoted to you. (56)
How many poets do not resort to the wife of Brahmā?
Or who does not become the husband of the goddess Śrī through whatever riches? O virtuous lady, having abandoned Mahādeva, you are the foremost among chaste women.
Even the embrace of the *kuravaka* tree by [her] two breasts is difficult to obtain.
Those who know the scriptures call the Goddess Śivā the wife of Druhiṇa (Brahmā),
Padmā the wife of Hari (Viṣṇu), and the Daughter of the Mountain the companion of Hara (Śiva).
You are some ineffable Fourth State (turiya), whose boundless majesty is difficult to comprehend;
O Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), Queen of the Supreme Brahman, you cause the universe to wander. Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī sport as the consorts of Brahmā and Hari.
With his beautiful form, he causes the devotion of Rati to slacken;
living for a long time, he has exhausted the entanglements of the bonds of the Paśus. (27a) Cirañjīvanneṣa kṣayitapaśupāśavyatikaraḥ.
One who devotes themselves to you experiences the essence known as the Supreme Brahman.
O Treasure, eternal, smiling, possessed of boundless qualities, skilled in ethics,
possessing unassailable knowledge, and the sole abode of a mind disciplined by restraint!
O You who are free from destiny, the object of praise within the entirety of the Upaniṣads,
the fearless and eternal— please accept this hymn of mine as well.
(By the phrase "this hymn of mine," he refutes the notion that the hymn possesses the quality of being well-composed.)
The rite of royal worship is performed by the rays of the lamps as if they were the sun;
nectar is offered through droplets of water from the moonstones;
and the ocean is satiated with its own waters.
O Mother, this praise of You is performed with my own words;
having thoroughly considered my purpose even beyond that, [I offer it]. 61. (27b)
Having understood another meaning, this is not to be censured.
Poets who travel upon a path that is exceedingly difficult to traverse become praiseworthy as they proceed ahead. (62)
O Mother, there has never been any distinction between you and Janārdana;
even devotion to the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha was established here by him. O Mother Bhavānī, nevertheless, I shall do as you desire.
May your compassionate side-glance never turn away from me. 63.
Thus ends the *Saundaryalaharī*. (28a)

1. Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇapati. Now follows the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). Herein is described the first sprout of supreme bliss and liberation, according to the Tantras, through the wondrous sequence of the six cakras and so forth.
In the region outside the Meru, the Moon and the Sun are seated on the left and the right respectively;

in the center is the Suṣumnā channel, consisting of the triad of the three qualities (guṇas) and having the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. Its form is more expansive than the Dhatura flower, extending from the middle of the root-knot to the head.
Named Vajrā, she emerges from the region of the face and spreads throughout the head, blazing in the center. In its midst is Citriṇī, radiant with the *praṇava*, accessible to yogis through yoga,
comparable to a thread of spider-silk, and situated within the center of Mount Meru amidst all the lotuses.
Having pierced through, it shines brilliantly by means of its composition as a stringing together [of letters], awakened by the pure Buddhas;
within that is the Brahma-nāḍī, situated inside the primordial deity from the cavity of the mouth of Hara.

Resplendent as a garland of lightning in the minds of sages, appearing in the form of shimmering threads, exceedingly subtle, awakened by pure knowledge, and consisting of the essence of all happiness— she shines forth as her own nature. At her mouth is the gateway to Brahman, a region delightful with the flowing stream of nectar.
They call this place of the knot the "mouth" of the channel known as Suṣumnā.
Now, the foundation lotus is attached to the mouth of the Suṣumnā;
it is located below the penis and above the anus, and possesses four petals.
With its face turned downward, it possesses a rising luster like the color of gold,
joined with the four Vedic syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *śa*.
Upon this earth is a four-cornered wheel;
with eight upward-pointing tridents it is an eight-cornered [mandala],
shining yellow in color, its body as tender as lightning.
Within that [space], the seed-syllable of the Earth (Dhara) is situated;
it is adorned with four arms, mounted upon the king of elephants and other [vehicles],
and possesses a radiance equal to the sun even without its lap [being occupied].
May the child who creates the universe, whose arms are the shining Vedas,
and whose lotus-face possesses the splendor of the four divisions [of the Vedas],
reside here; and may the goddess known as Ḍākinī also dwell herein.
With arms as radiant as the four Vedas and red eyes,
she possesses the splendor of many suns rising simultaneously;
she eternally bears the light of pure intellect.
The one called Vajra constantly dwells in the region of the mouth, situated in the center of the pericarp;
that corner is known as Traipura, shimmering like lightning, soft, and capable of assuming any desired form.
Within its center, the wind named Kandarpa blows perpetually on all sides;
there, the Lord of Life (Jīveśa), possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, shines, surpassing a cluster of Bandhujīva flowers.
In the midst of that, he exists in the form of a Liṅga, as tender as molten gold, facing the west.
The self-arisen radiance of knowledge and meditation, appearing in the form of a first sprout,

shines forth as the playful grace of the one who dwells in Kāśī; it laughs with a continuous stream of rays like a multitude of shimmering full moons, manifesting in the form of the whirlpools of the river.
Above that, a subtle thread of lotus-fiber, shimmering within the cavity, itself sweetly covers with its face the opening of the Brahma-door, enchanting the world. (30a)
Resembling a spiral conch, she is the abode of the playfulness of fresh, flickering garlands; she is like the river Sarayū when asleep, yet possesses a form of three coils shining upon Śiva.
She hums sweetly like the family-kuṇḍalinī, clearly manifest as a swarm of intoxicated bees.
Through the various sequences of distinctions in the composition of soft poetic verses,
she who is the life-force of the worlds is sustained by the breaking of their inhalations and exhalations.
She, possessing a form of intense radiance, sports within the cavity of her root-lotus.
In the midst of that is the Supreme (Parā), exceedingly subtle and most refined, who is supremely skilled in the supreme formless state (paramākala);
she is the mutual union of eternal bliss,
possessing a shimmering garland of rays that illuminate the entire vessel of the cosmic egg and all else.
(30b) May this Śrī Parameśvarī, who is the constant arising of supreme awakening, be victorious!
Having meditated upon this [reality] as shining like ten million suns within the cavity of the mūlacakra;
That king, a master of all sciences and a source of delight, possesses sovereign power and acts with sudden prowess.
His health is constant and boundless, and his inner self is filled with great bliss.
Possessing pure character, he honors even the teachers of all the gods with his speech and poetic compositions. (13)
Another lotus, beautiful and crimson with a stream of vermilion,
is fixed in the center of the *sauṣumna* at the base of the banner;
it is surrounded by limb-coverings and possesses the color of lightning.
With the syllables beginning with *rvv* and so forth, graced by the *bindu* and ending in *purandara*,
within that [space] shines a white radiance.
Then, there is the lotus mandala of Varuṇa,
charming in the form of a half-moon, as white as the autumnal moon;
it contains the stainless seed-syllable *vaṃ*, mounted upon the form of a sea-monster (*makara*).
Upon his lap may Hari protect [us], who possesses a charming grace,
who bears a splendor beautiful with the luster of a dark blue hue,
and who maintains the pride of being the first-born of the yellow-robed one (Brahmā).
Bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, with the Vedas held as his arms,
he shines here eternally; indeed, there Rākiṇī herself dwells, possessing a splendor of beauty like the interior of a blue lotus.

One who meditates upon this stainless lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, where the splendor of the limbs shines with hands raised holding various weapons, and which is adorned with divine garments and ornaments, and where the mind is intoxicated— [that lord of sages...]
(31b) For him, the entire host of enemies, beginning with the fault of egoism, is destroyed in that very instant.
That Lord of Yogis is like the sun, whose radiance dispels the wondrous darkness of delusion.
He composes with prose, verse, and literary compositions the splendor of a multitude of nectar-like poems.
Above that, at the base of the navel, in a region beautiful with ten petals and radiant as a full cloud,
the interior is filled with the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, accompanied by the moon, resembling blue lotuses.

One should meditate upon the red, triangular discus of Vaiśvānara, equal in size to the heart, surrounded on its exterior by three Svastikas; therein, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Fire.
One should then meditate upon [the deity] mounted upon a ram, resembling nine suns, with four arms and limbs ablaze.
In his lap shines eternally the form of Rudra, with the hue of pure vermilion;
his body is graced by the weight of ornaments consisting of ashes, and he is three-eyed in the form of Vṛṣadhara. (32a)
The bestower of desired objects to the worlds, whose hand is adorned with the granting of fearlessness, and who performs creation and dissolution—

therefore, she is Lākinī, the bringer of all auspiciousness, whose limbs blaze like the Vedas, who is dark-hued, clad in yellow garments and other finery, adorned with various ornaments, and whose mind is intoxicated.
Having meditated upon this, his navel-lotus becomes exceedingly active in creation, withdrawal, or preservation;
from the lotus of his mouth, Speech constantly shines forth, possessing the splendor of a mass of knowledge.
Above that, in his heart, is a most beautiful lotus, radiant with the luster of the bandhūka flower.
Offered by the twelve syllables beginning with *ka*, adorned with the hue of vermilion,
it is known by the name Anāhata; it is most excellent and possesses a radiance that exceeds all desire.
Here, one should meditate upon the mandala of Vāyu, resembling smoke and adorned with a hexagon;
in its center, one should contemplate the syllable of the Wind, sweet and grey like a column of smoke, beautifully mounted upon a black [bull] with four hands.

In the midst of that is the stainless treasury of compassion, named Īśa, with the luster of a swan; with his two hands he bestows the gestures of fearlessness and the supreme boon upon even the three worlds, and he is mounted upon Kṛṣṇa.
Here indeed resides Kākinī, possessing nine lightning-like yellow streaks, three eyes, and exceedingly beautiful.
Adorned with every ornament, she brings benefit to people with perfect joy;

in her hands she holds a noose, a beautiful trident, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. Intoxicated, her heart moistened by the essence of full nectar, she wears a garland of skeletons.
(33a) This [power] called the Triangle, shimmering within the pericarp of the lotus,
resides therein; its form is as delicate as the tip of a flash of lightning.

One should meditate in the heart-lotus upon that which is called *vaṇā*, a *śivaliṅga* resplendent with a golden-colored unguent, like the sun shining with its subtle radiance, the abode of the glory of supreme splendor;
[one should meditate] upon the celestial tree, the seat and abode of all.
Adorned by the swan-like flame of the lamp of the god Anila,
it bears the splendor of the shimmering filaments within the orb of the Sun;
the Lord of Speech, though the Sovereign of the worlds, is capable both of protecting and destroying them.
The Lord of Yogins is the most beloved of those dear to the Blessed Lady;
he is the master of knowledge, his host of senses is conquered, and he is capable of focused concentration in meditation. (33b)
Constantly raining down streams of poetry through prose and the words of verse, it is the deity of the body’s fortune, possessing the power to enter another's body in an instant.
[5] At the throat is the pure lotus called Viśuddha, stainless yet appearing with a smoky hue. [6]
The circle of the sky, appearing like the full moon, was illuminated by all the vowels, which shone forth from the petals of the lamp-like intellect; it took the form of a circle,
while the white-colored vowels shone upon the body of the serpent of frost-like luster.
He whose limbs are adorned with arms resplendent with the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and the goad,
and who dwells eternally upon the lap of Manas, his body inseparable from Girijā and white as snow.
Three-eyed, five-faced, adorned with ten graceful arms and clad in a tiger-skin garment,
the primordial deity is eternally renowned and established as Śiva.
In the ocean of nectar, within a pure lotus, resides the goddess Sākinī, radiant and dressed in yellow garments.
Holding an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad in her four lotus-like hands,

she bears upon the pericarp of her ear the full orb of the moon, devoid of its spots— the gateway to liberation from delusions for that Śrī who is beyond the head [of Brahmā] and whose senses are pure.
In this state, having established the mind without limit and attained complete yoga,
that poet becomes eloquent, wise, and a truly perfected practitioner with a tranquil heart;
he becomes the lord of the three worlds, the benefactor of all, and liberated from disease, sorrow, and the like.
(34b) He is long-lived, living without end, the light for the swan amidst the supreme darkness. 4.
The lotus of his command is illuminated by the splendor of meditation, which is like the sun to the moon.
Her body is radiant with two eyes that are like the sun and moon; her eye-petals are brilliantly white.
In their midst is Hākinī, as white as the moon, possessing six faces.
In her hands she holds the Vidyā-mudrā, a hand-drum, and a rosary, her mind intoxicated.

Within the interior of this lotus, the mind shines forth in its subtle form; it is well known to reside in the womb, within the pericarp, as the other state of Śiva, manifesting the mark of the *liṅga*.
It is the play of garlands of lightning, the supreme station of *Kula*, and the awakening of the *Brahmasūtra*.
One whose heart is most steadfast should contemplate that primordial seed-syllable of the Vedas in its proper sequence;
through the nature of meditation, the supreme adept becomes a lord of sages who moves swiftly into the city of another.
The omniscient one, belonging to all lands, the benefactor of all, the knower of all scriptures,
the master of the practice of non-duality, he who has shattered the supreme, unprecedented,
and established [doctrines] of others— may even he, long-lived and the creator within the abode of the three worlds, be intent upon its preservation. (3)
Within that wheel, the pure inner self of the awakened ones dwells eternally;
it is the letter *pra*, whose form is the arrangement of the *praṇava* and whose light is like a lamp.
Above that is the half-moon, and above that is the letter *ma*, which has the form of a shimmering bindu.
Above that, this *nāda* shines forth like a continuous stream of the most excellent and sublime nectar.
When the mind has dissolved into this state, the abode of supreme bliss, it attains the ultimate.
Having bound the breath in the objectless state, as well-known through the oral instructions of the supreme guru, the yogi,
through constant practice, perceives the subtle powers of the winds;
he also beholds the stages of yoga whose forms shine forth within the midst of those very powers.
Having the form of a blazing island, it is also intensely radiant like the newly risen sun; or rather, it is a light of brilliance meeting the sky and the earth in their midst.
In this place, the Blessed One, possessed of full majesty, becomes manifest.
Rāhu is the witness to the eclipse of the moon and the sun, like a spear; here,
at this place of Viṣṇu, which is sweet with incomparable and supreme fragrance,
having offered up my life-breaths while my mind is filled with joy at the end of my life, [I shall depart].
The lord of yogis enters that supreme, eternal, divine Person— unborn, primordial, ancient, and known through the Vedanta— who is the source of the three worlds.
Above that is the abode of Vāyu, and further above is the form of Great Bliss (Mahānanda).
It is half of Śiva, having the form of Śiva—tranquil, bestowing boons and fearlessness, and radiant with the perfected Buddha.
When the yogi, whose conduct is well-disciplined through service to the lotus-feet of the Guru’s pair, beholds this...
May the perfection of that dwelling always rest upon the palm of his hand.
Above that, on a peak of the Śaṅkhinī in a secluded place,
there shines clearly a lotus with a thousand petals below the Visarga, as radiant as the full moon.
With its face turned downward, peaceful, possessing the mass of filaments with the beauty of a crescent moon,
its body radiant with the letters beginning with *la* on the forehead and so forth, it is of the nature of absolute bliss.
Within that [space], there resides the pure, full moon, devoid of its spots;
it possesses a mass of shimmering moonlight and laughs with a continuous stream of gentle rays.
Within that, a triangle constantly flashes, having the form of lightning.
Within that [space] is a subtle [receptacle], served and worshipped by all the hosts of gods;
it is most secret, a mass of supreme fragrance arising from the sound (nāda),
the supreme subtle vessel, possessing the form of the full moon and radiant.
In this place resides the God, renowned as the perfected one known as Paramaśiva;
he is the essential nature, the soul of all, accompanied by the poison of aesthetic essence, the swan blinded by the delusion of ignorance.
O Nṛmalamati, the Lord Hari, the master of all, who bestows a continuous stream of nectar and is supremely intent on bestowing self-knowledge upon the ascetic,
remains seated as the source of the entire succession of happiness.
He is known by the name Haṃsa Paramahaṃsa.
Some regard him as the abode of Śiva, while the Vaiṣṇava groups consider him the Supreme Person; thus, most identify him with the state of Hari and Hara, though others do not.
The foot of the Goddess, which is a shower of bliss from the pair of the Goddess’s feet,
is the stainless abode of Prakṛti and Puruṣa even for other lords of sages.
Having known this abode here, the best of men, with his own thoughts restrained, [attains liberation].
May that virtuous man of disciplined mind never again be slain anywhere in the three worlds throughout the cycle of existence; may his power remain entirely intact. (37b)
Always [capable of] acting... even the movement of birds and pure speech [are surpassed].
Here resides that sixteenth digit of the moon, which is like a young sun;
it is pure, subtle as a hundredth part of a fiber from a lotus stalk, and is the supreme [Prakṛti].
She whose body is as delicate as a flash of lightning, who is eternally risen with her face turned downward,
whose lips are the vessel of nectar flowing from the supreme mutual union of perfect bliss—
she dwells within that, the supreme beyond the supreme, known as the digit of Nirvāṇa.
The Blessed Lady, whose nature is ever-arisen awakening, is the presiding deity of all beings, like a single hair-tip split a thousandfold. (38a)
Bent like the crescent of the moon and possessing a luster equal to all the suns,
the supreme power of perfect nirvāṇa shines in her central region;
she is as radiant as ten million suns, the mother of the three worlds, whose single form is composed of ten million parts.
She is more secret than the tip of a hair, bearing an endless stream of flowing love;
she is the life-force of all, eternally carrying the awakening to reality within the minds of sages. Within her midst lies the stainless, eternal state of Śiva, attainable through yoga.
Some of the most wise ones, indeed, speak of that state called Nityānanda, which consists of all happiness and is of the nature of pure consciousness, as the Vaiṣṇava state known as Brahman. (38b)
Some virtuous ones consider this [state] to be the swan-eyed [vision], while others regard it as liberation, self-awakening,

or the Goddess herself through the syllable *HŪṂ*. A man of excellent character, having learned from the mouth of the venerable Lord both the Krama and the illumination of the reality of great liberation— which consists of the constant practice of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*)— [attains it].
In the center of the Brahma-gate, he of pure enlightened nature creates for the virtuous;
having pierced that form of the *liṅga* through the union of wind and fire,
and by that very sequence, having pierced the three *liṅgas*, [he enters] Śiva, the supreme essence, in the subtle abode which is like a lamp.
That Goddess, whose form is like a shimmering thread of pure being, is her very nature;
she shines forth, having attained that which is called Brahman, the auspicious Śiva, who is adorned with all things.

And she brings about the essential nature of the bliss of liberation through the subtle moment of the stars. At the conclusion of the dissolution, the wise one, together with the *jīva*, should contemplate the Kulakuṇḍalinī—
the Mistress in the supreme Śiva-abode, the pure lotus-palace at the gateway to liberation.

The lord of yogis, resting upon the pair of lotus-feet of his Guru, meditates in samādhi upon the Supreme Goddess, who bestows desired fruits and whose form is pure consciousness. Then, having drunk the supreme nectar, which is the color of lac, from the Paraśiva, Kuṇḍalinī [awakens].
The beautiful one, who is the root-luster of the path of the Kula and the great manifestation of full bliss,
should satisfy the deity with a steady mind by means of that divine stream of nectar.
The yogi, whose lineage of yoga is unknown, having realized this supreme sequence situated within the vessel of the universe,
with mind restrained and disciplined by the restraints (yamas) and other practices,
may he— awakened by the touch of the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru— bestow compassion.
He is indeed born in saṃsāra, yet he is never subject to decay at the time of dissolution;
rejoicing in a succession of perfect bliss, he is the foremost among the virtuous. The yogi, established in his true nature, practices yoga by night, at the twilights, and likewise by day.
This stainless, pure, and well-guarded sequence is the primary cause for the knowledge of liberation.
For one whose internal mind is fixed upon the pair of lotus feet of the venerable Guru, his heart inevitably dances within the state of his chosen deity. (21)
(40a) Thus ends the *Antaryajana*.
First comes birth-impurity (*jātasūtaka*), and at the end, death-impurity (*mṛtasūtaka*).
A mantra that is joined with the two *sūtaka*s does not succeed. Having rendered the mantra devoid of beginning and end, one should indeed repeat it mentally;
thus freed from the two *sūtaka*s, the mantra bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Having performed the beneficial rite there in the evening, one should indeed recite the mantra with focused intellect.
Free from the two types of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the mantra, together with its ritual success, [bestows results].
That which is the impurity of birth is above; that which is the impurity of death is below.
(40b) 1. Homage to the Glorious Guru.
[The [vital breath] is dissolved] in the Bindu, in the Rodhinī which is half of that, in the Nāda, and in the very end of the Nāda.
Furthermore, when Śakti is all-pervasive,
one should contemplate the wheel in three ways within the sphere of Samanā and Unmanā, and indeed within the Great Bindu:
namely, the letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the Bindu itself.
The Half-Moon is dissolved in the Nāda, and the End of Sound (Nādānta) likewise;
then there is Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.
At the end of Samanā is the net of bonds (pāśajāla), and at the end of Unmanā is Paraśiva.

(41a) Nirodhikā is the half-moon; [she resides] in the state of the drop and its digit. In the sphere of the *dhruva* at the end of sound and beyond sound, she is in the state of poison, in the transmental (*unmanī*), as the Supreme Śiva. Now, the fourteen worlds.
1. Meditation on the Thousand-Petaled [Lotus]:

Upon the head, in the lotus situated in space which possesses all its petals, one should meditate on that Bhairavī known as Yakṣiṇī, whose hands shine with all weapons and who is the synthesis of all colors.

I meditate upon the Ḍākinī, who has seven faces, who bestows all happiness, whose nature is that of all the elements, whose mind is attached to all food, who is consecrated by the Supreme Śiva, and who possesses every form. [This is] the meditation on the six cakras.
In the moon-lotus between the eyebrows, which shines with two petals and possesses white-colored hands,
she holds the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), a *ḍamaru* drum, a rosary, and a skull-cup. (41b)
One should meditate upon that Hākinī, who has six faces, is established in the Arjuna tree, is adorned with three eyes, is accompanied by Haṃsavatī and others,
is intent upon turmeric-rice, and is praised by all the gods.
She has a red body and red eyes, causes fear to the ignorant folk, and holds a trident and a khaṭvāṅga in her hands.
One should meditate on [the goddess] holding a skull-bowl in her left hand and a wine-filled chalice, possessing a single face;
she is exceedingly fierce with terrifying fangs, the destroyer of the host of enemies, and intent upon milk-rice offerings.
One should visualize her body surrounded at the neck by the Ḍākinīs, beginning with Mṛtā.
(42a) Śāmā has a trident and a lotus in her hands, and she carries a *ḍamaru* drum and a sharp wheel;
she is wide-faced, red in color, and three-eyed, with frowning brows and bared fangs that terrify the wicked, and she shines with radiant splendors.

One should meditate upon her as radiant, seated within the lotus-heart of the God of gods, the sole mistress of the blood-element; intent upon the three pure [objects], delighted by the intoxication of honey, and gracious. When [the deity] is black, one should meditate on the Goddess as three-faced, beautiful with three eyes, fanged, and of fierce form.
Having meditated on her— holding a vajra, a spear, and a staff in her right hands, and bestowing fearlessness and boons in her left hands—
brought from the lotus at the navel, which shines with a ten-petalled pericarp.
The supreme adept should meditate upon her whose heart is eager for the enjoyment of meat and molasses.
In the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, beautiful with six petals, he should visualize her who has four faces and three eyes,
whose complexion is yellow, and who holds a trident, a rosary, a skull-bowl, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

One should meditate upon her as Kākinī, who is established in the element of fat, who is free from pride and delight, who is eternal and beyond [all worldly] states, and who bestows the fruit of supreme intoxication upon those whose minds are intent on her.
One should contemplate the Goddess, whose nature is light, who possesses three eyes and five faces, and who has beautiful fangs.
(43a) Holding in her lotus-like hands a sugarcane bow, a goad, a book, and the gesture of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*),
she who intoxicates the people— both those with crests and those like beasts— is seated upon the bones within the lotus located at the *mūlādhāra*.
One should meditate upon her as being full of joy regarding mung-bean rice, bestowing honey and clarified butter, and being gracious.
